title: Accent Is the Last Acceptable Prejudice in British Workplaces
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian argues that accent is the overlooked filter shaping who gets heard, promoted, and sponsored in British organisations. He opens with a thought experiment in which two candidates give identical interview answers and the one with Received Pronunciation is remembered as more credible. Drawing on the 2022 Sutton Trust report Speaking Up, he cites findings such as a quarter of professionals being mocked or singled out for their accent, rising to 29 percent among working-class senior managers. Accent works as a proxy for class, education, and competence, and because it is not a protected characteristic under the Equality Act it is neither measured nor managed. The bias is hard to challenge because those who hold it experience it as a legitimate quality judgement rather than prejudice. He notes that awareness reduces the effect and challenges leaders to ask whose voice is literally missing from their leadership teams.
points: Accent bias persists in part because it is invisible to formal diversity reporting, unlike gender pay gaps or board ethnicity, which are tracked and published.
Evaluators feel their reaction to an accent as discernment about polish or leadership material, which is why the bias resists challenge.
Karian frames accent bias as class bias with better deniability, so organisations that track gender and ethnicity but ignore accent may still be filtering by background.
The research suggests the problem is amenable to simple interventions, because recruiters who were told about accent bias narrowed their differential ratings.
Leaders can start by measuring accent-related experiences and examining who sits at the top table, rather than assuming inclusion work already covers it.
quotes: Twenty-five percent of professionals report being mocked, criticised, or singled out in work settings because of their accent.
Accent functions as a proxy. They state that it acts as a cognitive shortcut through which listeners infer social class, educational background, and by extension, professional credibility.

Unlike racial or gender discrimination, which most people recognise as wrong even when they practice it, accent discrimination is frequently experienced by those who perpetrate it as a legitimate quality judgement.
The bias feels like discernment rather than prejudice. That is precisely what makes it so resistant to challenge.
When recruiters are explicitly told that accent bias is a documented problem, the differential ratings of accented candidates narrow significantly.
Accent bias is, ultimately, class bias with better deniability.
The organisations spending significant sums on inclusion might usefully ask themselves: whose voice, literally, is missing from our leadership? And why.
